Dishonour
dĭs-ŏn´ur
n., v. (disgrace; rendering Greek atimia)
Dis- with honour. Dishonour is honour withheld or reversed, and Paul makes it a category in both the potter's house and the resurrection.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dishonour is disgrace. Christ says, “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house” (Mat 13:57), and tells His accusers, “I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me” (Joh 8:49). Paul asks the Jews who boast in the law, “through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?” (Rom 2:23). He describes vessels “one to honour, and another unto dishonour” (Rom 9:21), and says the body “is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory” (1Co 15:43).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dishonor as reproach; disgrace; ignominy; shame; whatever constitutes a stain or blemish in the reputation.

expand to see more

DISHONOR, n. Reproach; disgrace; ignominy; shame; whatever constitutes a stain or blemish in the reputation.

DISHONOR, v.t. To disgrace; to bring reproach or shame on; to stain the character of; to lessen reputation.

2. To treat with indignity.

Key Scripture

Joh 8:49 — "Jesus answered, I have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me."

Rom 2:23 — "Thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?"

1Co 15:43 — "It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:"

Mat 13:57 — "And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house."

Modern Corruption

Believers guard their own honour and are careless with God's, and Paul asks a religious audience whether their law-breaking dishonours the God they boast in.

expand to see more

Romans 2:23-24 aims at the religiously respectable: thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God? For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you. The dishonour is not done by the world's opposition but by the inconsistency of God's own people, and the damage lands on His reputation among outsiders. That is a heavier charge than any the passage makes against pagans.

1 Corinthians 15:43 uses the word without any moral sting: it is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory. Paul is describing burial. A corpse is dishonourable in the plain sense — it must be covered and put away — and the resurrection is stated as the reversal of exactly that condition. The verse dignifies grief by naming the indignity honestly before promising its undoing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek atimia (G819), dishonour, shame; atimazo (G818), to dishonour; time (G5092), honour — the positive term.

expand to see more

Greek atimazo (G818) — to dishonour; John 8:49, Romans 2:23, James 2:6.

Greek atimia (G819) — dishonour; Romans 9:21, 1 Corinthians 15:43, 2 Timothy 2:20.

Greek time (G5092) — honour, price; the contrasting term throughout.

Usage

"“I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me” — the charge answered plainly."

"“Through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?” — aimed at the religious."

"“Sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory” — the indignity named before its undoing."
